title: Live walkthrough: Hosted chat, streaming and error-handling patterns
summary: AE + SE run a hosted API demo focused on chat generation, streaming behavior, request params, and retry/backoff patterns. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for a multi-tenant analytics product; main concerns: latency, deterministic billing, audit logs, and retry semantics for intermittent 5xxs.
next_steps: Samir to send pricing comparison (hosted vs dedicated) and example SLA language
Leah to share console screenshots and a quick runbook for retry strategies
Maya to share a representative API payload and p99 latency targets
Schedule a technical POC call with their SREs week of 2025-04-14
action_items: Samir: Send pricing + SLA examples by 2025-04-08
Leah: Export console dashboard screenshots and token cost breakdown by 2025-04-06
Maya: Provide sample payloads and p99 targets by 2025-04-07
transcript:
[00:00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, were Samir, AE on the Redwood team, with Leah and Carlos from solutions.
[00:00:08] Jorge: Hi, Jorge here, CTO at CloudScale Analytics. Were mainly evaluating hosted first and maybe dedicated later.
[00:00:15] Samir: Great, quick agenda: high-level hosted API demo for chat/text generation, show streaming, discuss params, and then do retry/backoff patterns and show the console cost view and Optimize suggestions. Sound good?
[00:00:27] Maya: Yep that works. We want to see typical latencies and how retries behave under transient 5xxs.
[00:00:35] Leah: Awesome. A quick callout: well show the SDK and REST examples; the behavior is the same. Also well point out how streaming chunks arrive and how we handle partial responses on retries.
[00:00:47] Samir: Ok starting the demo. (typing) Heres the typical chat request we send: model, messages array, temperature, max_tokens, and stream=true to receive server-sent events.
[00:00:59] Carlos: Well show a short prompt so you can see chunking. Notice were sending a short system message and a user message. Stream will emit partial deltas every 50-200ms depending on generation.
[00:01:12] (screen share starts) 
[00:01:20] Leah: Youll see in the terminal the SSE lines coming in: data: {"id":"tok_...","delta":"The"} then next chunk " data: {\"delta\":\" model\" }" — transcription sometimes shows extra whitespace, but thats normal.
[00:01:36] Maya: Does the stream guarantee order? If we get network hiccups can chunks arrive out of order?
[00:01:43] Leah: Good question. The stream is ordered over the TCP/SSE connection; if the connection drops and you reconnect we currently resume with a short token-level resume not full delta replay. For full-resume semantics we recommend prefix caching + idempotent request keys so the client can reconcile.
[00:02:02] Samir: The practical pattern we recommend: use request_id in metadata, keep prefix caching on the server side (we can enable automatic prefix/KV cache per route), and on reconnect fetch the last confirmed token index.
[00:02:16] Jorge: When you say prefix caching, do you mean you cache conversation history on the server or on the model runtime?
[00:02:22] Leah: Its runtime-level KV cache plus optional prefix cache in the edge layer. That reduces token cost because we avoid re-sending long histories — we send a short pointer instead. Note: we also do model-aware kernel selection so the latency per token varies by architecture.
[00:02:36] Alex (SRE): Curious on how rewrites affect billing. If we reconnect and the model regenerates, do we double-bill for tokens sent twice?
[00:02:44] Carlos: Billing is per-token generated by the model instance that completed. If a partial response was aborted we bill for tokens actually produced; retries that re-generate generally increment consumed tokens. In practice prefix caching prevents most duplicated generation.
[00:02:59] Priya: Ok, walk me through params: temperature, top_p, stop sequences. How do those influence streaming?
[00:03:06] Leah: temperature/top_p influence sampling; streaming still emits tokens as theyre sampled. Higher temp increases variability and may change chunk sizes slightly because tokens are sampled differently. stop sequences are enforced by the runtime; we truncate or emit final chunk with stop token.
[00:03:21] Maya: Can you demo a change in temperature live?
[00:03:24] Samir: Sure, Ill send two requests side-by-side. (types) Temp 0.0 vs temp 0.9 — youll see the 0.0 is conservative and shorter, 0.9 is more verbose.
[00:03:38] (both streams start) 
[00:03:44] Maya: I can already see the 0.9 run generating more digressions. Ok thats helpful.
[00:03:50] Leah: Also note max_tokens is a hard cap — once hit the stream ends with an EOS event.
[00:03:56] Samir: Now switching to error/retry patterns — common question. We typically advise exponential backoff with jitter for HTTP 429 and 5xx, but with idempotency keys for POST-generation calls.
[00:04:07] Jorge: Idempotency keys — do you mean the client should supply one and you dedupe on the backend?
[00:04:12] Carlos: Exactly. You include x-request-id or our idempotency header; if the server receives the same key it can return the prior result if available, or resume generation if it failed mid-way depending on config.
[00:04:23] Alex: What about partial outputs? If a job was partially generated and we retry, how do we get the rest without redoing earlier tokens?
[00:04:30] Leah: Two patterns: resume token-based where runtime stores KV cache and last token index keyed to idempotency key, or client-side merge where client stores the last confirmed chunk. For most customers runtime resume + prefix caching works best.
[00:04:43] Priya: Do you have built-in client libraries that handle reconnects and SSE parsing?
[00:04:48] Samir: Yes, SDKs for JS/Python include stream helpers and an auto-reconnect example. They also include a sample RetryPolicy class that implements exponential backoff with jitter and respects Retry-After headers.
[00:04:59] Jorge: Can you show the console where token/cost breakdown is visible? We want to understand per-route cost and tracing.
[00:05:05] (screen shifts to Console) 
[00:05:12] Leah: Heres the Console route for your dev workspace. We show per-request token count, model variant, latency p50/p95/p99, and a cost column. You can filter by route, by model, and by time window.
[00:05:27] Maya: Is there a way to link back to the trace of the request and see the SSE timeline?
[00:05:31] Carlos: Yes, click into a request, youll see raw request/response payloads, and the event stream log. We also surface errors with stack traces when theres an internal runtime failure.
[00:05:43] Priya: How are quotas applied? We will have multiple tenants inside our app.
[00:05:48] Samir: You can configure per-api-key quotas, per-route limits, and tenant tags. For multi-tenant apps we recommend per-tenant API keys routed to the same model but with rate limiting enforced at the edge.
[00:06:00] Jorge: Can the Console show cost per customer? Wed want billing attribution.
[00:06:04] Leah: Yes — tag requests with tenant_id metadata and then use the billing view to break down tokens and cost by tag. The Optimize tool will also recommend batching or caching opportunities per tenant.
[00:06:16] Maya: Quick question on retries: do you ever recommend synchronous retries vs background job re-sends? For a chat UI we want near realtime.
[00:06:23] Carlos: For interactive chat, synchronous small retries (2-3 attempts with short backoff) are normal. For longer running reranks or heavy prompts move to async jobs with a websocket or webhook notification when ready.
[00:06:36] Priya: How do function calls (tooling) interact with streaming? We plan to use tool calling to fetch DB snippets.
[00:06:43] Leah: Function/tool calling can be streamed too but typically you get an object payload at the end that indicates the chosen function. We stream the partial reasoning until the call; once function is invoked youll see a function_call delta with name and arguments.
[00:06:56] Maya: Sometimes our tool args are large. Any advice to keep args compact to prevent long token resends on retries?
[00:07:03] Leah: Keep tool results small and reference large blobs by id (signed url or pointer). The runtime supports pointer tokenization where you pass metadata instead of full payload.
[00:07:12] Samir: Ok jump to a live transient 5xx demo — Ill simulate a 502 between the model and runtime. (types) This is important: when we return a 502 the client should backoff and then request with the same idempotency key so runtime can return a successful outcome if it completed.
[00:07:30] (simulated failure emitted) 
[00:07:40] Maya: I see the client got a 502, then after 2 retries a successful response. Tokens look similar, did we double bill?
[00:07:47] Carlos: You can see in Console the first failed attempt shows tokens billed for partial generation, the final successful attempt shows only tokens for the completion. The runtime attempts to avoid duplicate full-generation via resume logic but partial tokens can be billed.
[00:08:02] Alex: Are there SLA guarantees around transient errors? Our legal team will ask.
[00:08:07] Samir: For hosted we have uptime SLAs on dedicated plans; for transient errors we track p99 error budgets and include operational SLOs. Ill include the exact SLA language in the follow-up.
[00:08:17] Priya: Can you show Optimize suggestions — batching and caching recs?
[00:08:21] (Console -> Optimize tab) 
[00:08:26] Leah: Heres Optimize analyzing a week of traffic. It surfaced that 23% of requests are similar prefixes and recommended prefix caching which could reduce token usage by ~30% for that route. It also recommended a batching window of 30ms for small inference calls that can be batched without hurting p50 latency.
[00:08:44] Maya: Do you have guardrails for batching latency? We cant allow p99 to spike above 300ms.
[00:08:50] Carlos: Optimize simulates latency tradeoffs and estimates p99. You can set latency SLOs and it will only recommend batching profiles that meet those constraints.
[00:08:59] Jorge: What about quantized model variants — any difference for streaming or retries?
[00:09:04] Leah: Quantized variants generally have slightly different token throughput and may affect sampling timing; retry and idempotency semantics are identical. The Console shows model-variant-specific perf numbers so you can pick the right variant.
[00:09:15] Maya: Can we pin a model version and do canary rollouts?
[00:09:19] Samir: Yes, you can pin and create rollout policies—canary, A/B, or percentage-based. Console lets you shift traffic and watch quality metrics tied to eval sets.
[00:09:29] Priya: About logging and compliance — we need audit logs and SSO.
[00:09:33] Samir: We support SSO/SAML, RBAC, and audit logs with retention options. We also integrate KMS for envelope encryption and can deploy Private if you need on-prem or VPC with HSM.
[00:09:46] Jorge: Good. What about rate limits for streaming connections? Our users may open many parallel streams.
[00:09:52] Leah: We have connection-level limits plus token-rate limits. You can whitelist specific clients with higher connection allowances. For heavy concurrent connections Dedicated is better.
[00:10:02] Maya: Could you show an example of the SDK's streaming handler that merges delta chunks and handles reconnects?
[00:10:07] Carlos: Sure, switching back to code. (screen) Heres the JS helper: onmessage parse SSE, append delta to buffer, emit to UI, track last_confirmed_index in localstorage. On reconnect, re-request with same idempotency key and use resume token header to fetch the remaining tokens.
[00:10:25] Maya: That looks straightforward. Any gotchas with mobile clients?
[00:10:29] Leah: Mobile often has flaky networks; youll want to reduce chunk frequency (bigger deltas) and rely on prefix caching and resumability. Also watch websocket timeouts — SSE over HTTP/2 works better for some mobile stacks.
[00:10:42] Priya: Are there known transcription or model-name mismatches in logs? We saw some odd model IDs in our test logs.
[00:10:48] Samir: Sometimes internal model variant tags differ (e.g., rdx-v1-q8 vs rdx-1-quant). Console normalizes this but raw logs can have engine ids. Were improving naming consistency.
[00:10:59] Jorge: Ok wrapping up — can we get sample latency numbers that match the demo environment? Were targeting p99 < 350ms for short prompts.
[00:11:06] Leah: On our hosted low-latency variants, typical p99 is 150-300ms for small prompts (<128 tokens) in NA regions. Ill send our perf matrix and the benchmark harness so you can run against representative traffic.
[00:11:20] Samir: Quick recap and next steps. Were going to: (1) Send pricing comparison and SLA (Samir), (2) Share console screenshots, SDK streaming example, and retry runbook (Leah), (3) Customer to share sample payloads and p99 targets (Maya). Also schedule POC call with SREs.
[00:11:37] Jorge: Sounds good. One last thing — can you include a short note about cost per 1k tokens for the hosted plan vs dedicated reserved? We need a rough TCO.
[00:11:45] Samir: Absolutely. Ill include a couple scenarios in the email.
[00:11:49] (small wrap-up chat) 
[00:11:58] Maya: Thanks everyone, this was very helpful.
[00:12:01] Samir: Thanks all, well follow up. Bye.
